recentItems.title: How 9/11 transformed US foreign policy over 25 years: Analysis
recentItems.description:
Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, Richard Weitz, a senior fellow at the NATO Defence College and security analyst at Wikistrat, reflects on that day and its lasting impact. He recalls the confusion after the first plane hit, before the scale of the attacks became clear once the second plane struck and the Pentagon was hit.

Weitz says the biggest change since has been the shift in US foreign policy, from the hopeful, domestically focused 1990s to an extraordinarily interventionist era. The US invasion of Afghanistan was understandable, he says, but the subsequent war in Iraq created problems, including with Iran, that persist today. He also argues the US "dropped the ball" on China and Russia, allowing both to become potential adversaries.

recentItems.title: Trump heads to Ireland for diplomacy and golf amid planned protests
recentItems.description:
US President Donald Trump is visiting Ireland on Saturday, combining diplomacy with a trip to his own golf resort. He will meet Ireland's prime minister and president at state residences in Dublin's Phoenix Park, before heading west to Doonbeg, which is hosting the Irish Open, keeping him away from planned protests in the capital.

Polls suggest most Irish people oppose the visit, but economic ties with the US run deep. 

Independent businesses have felt the fallout from Trump's tariffs, with shop owner Clare Grennan describing the scramble to keep shipping to American customers. Protesters, including lawmaker Richard Boyd Barrett, cite anger over Trump's role in the war in Gaza, strong Irish support for Palestinians, and rising energy and fuel costs.

Al Jazeera's Milena Veselinovic reports from Dublin.

recentItems.title: Russia's strikes on Kyiv fuel stations mark a new phase of war
recentItems.description:
Russia's drone and missile campaign against Ukraine appears to be entering a new phase, with strikes over the past two days targeting fuel stations in Kyiv, another sign the air campaign against the capital is expanding.

On Thursday, an air strike hit a petrol station in Kyiv. By the time journalists arrived, the injured had already been taken to hospital and clean-up was under way. 

On Friday, Russia hit two more stations, with a double strike on one, a drone followed fifteen minutes later by another. 

All the stations hit belong to the state company Ukrnafta and are among 18 Kyiv fuel stations identified as targets in intercepted Russian communications. Motorists in the city say they now plan routes around air-raid alerts, calling it one more threat to already precarious lives.

Al Jazeera's Rory Challands reports from Kyiv.
